title: Rate Limiting Strategies
description: Learn rate limiting strategies to protect microservices from abuse and ensure fair usage.

data.text: Rate limiting protects microservices from abuse, prevents cascading failures, and ensures fair usage. Amazon, Google, and Stripe all enforce rate limits on their APIs to maintain service quality and prevent expensive overloads.

Without rate limiting, a single abusive client or a sudden traffic spike can overwhelm your services, causing cascading failures across the system. Rate limits act as a circuit breaker at the gateway level, protecting downstream services.

data.title: Common Algorithms
items: Token bucket: Tokens are added at a fixed rate; requests consume tokens
Leaky bucket: Requests are queued and processed at a fixed rate
Fixed window: Count requests in fixed time windows (e.g., per minute)
Sliding window: Smooth counting over rolling windows to avoid burst issues

data.title: Rate Limit Headers
data.text: Always return rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset) so clients can adapt their request rate programmatically.

items.question: Where should I implement rate limiting?
items.answer: At the API Gateway is best. It protects all downstream services. You can also add per-service rate limits for critical resources.

items.question: What is a reasonable rate limit?
items.answer: It depends on your service. Public APIs often allow 100-1000 requests per minute per user. Internal services may have higher limits.

items.question: Should I use a distributed rate limiter?
items.answer: Yes, if you have multiple gateway instances. Use Redis or a similar distributed store to share rate limit state across instances.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Rate limiting protects services from abuse and overload
Token bucket and sliding window are the most common algorithms
Implement at the API Gateway for maximum protection
data.takeaway: Rate limiting is essential for production microservices; implement it early.
